problem: Existing VLN-CE models, including monocular-RGB VLM-based VLA navigators such as NaVid, Uni-NaVid, NaVILA and StreamVLN, cannot recover once they deviate from the instructed path. A few imperfect step-wise predictions compound into failure. Prior correction approaches (SmartWay backtracking with a closed-source LLM, EvolveNav chain-of-thought) add extra modules or long inference, which hurts real-robot deployment.
motivation: Most prior work tries to make every step correct by improving representations or scaling data, yet deviations are unavoidable. After a deviation the robot faces a scene that no longer matches the instruction. The driving observation is that a well-trained navigator still fails on many episodes of its own training set. Those failures come with ground-truth reference paths, so they are a free, automatically labelable source of recovery data, and correction ability can be trained implicitly without slowing inference.
key_idea: Repeatedly evaluate the model on its training split, locate where each trajectory first leaves the oracle path, turn those points into recovery trajectories (via a planner) plus MLLM-generated keyframe perception data, and continue training on them; iterate this 'Self-correction Flywheel'.
insight: Failures on the training set are high-value, cheaply labeled data: re-planning from the deviation point teaches recovery actions that oracle-only imitation never shows. In the 1st-iteration ablation (Table 2), removing error-correcting trajectories hurts most (R2R-CE SR 63.0→59.2, RxR-CE SR 63.1→60.7). Removing keyframe perception QA/captions (60.1/61.0) or the data-mixing/sampling strategy (60.0/62.2) also hurts, so both 'what to do' and 'why' supervision matter. Iterating the flywheel keeps generating fresh errors and improves both benchmarks for three rounds before degrading at round four (shown only in a figure). The final model's RxR-CE SR (69.3) is far above the 1-iteration model (63.1), suggesting most gains come from repeated iterations rather than the first round.
method: VLA backbone: SigLIP vision encoder + 2-layer MLP projector + Qwen2 LLM, initialized from LLaVA-Video 7B. Takes 16 sampled monocular RGB frames plus the instruction and autoregressively outputs an action chunk (4 effective actions).

Navigation fine-tuning: >2.1M step-wise action-prediction samples from VLN-CE R2R (527K) and RxR (1.58M) train oracle trajectories, with domain randomization (camera height, FOV, resolution, illumination).

Auxiliary tasks: trajectory-based instruction generation (10K R2R + 20K RxR full trajectories → instruction), plus general multimodal data recall (240K ActivityNet-QA/NextQA samples from LLaVA-Video-178K) to prevent forgetting.

Deviation detection: interpolate the oracle reference points; per robot position compute the distance h_i to the densified path and its foot point P_i. The deviation point M_t is the first timestep with h_t > threshold S, with all earlier h_i ≤ S.

Error-correcting trajectories: if P_t lies on segment G_k→G_{k+1}, a trajectory planner generates T_e=(M_t, G_{k+1}, …, G_n). The action loss applies only on T_e, and the pre-deviation trajectory serves as observation history.

Keyframe perception data: frames at, before and after M_t are fed to Qwen-VL-Plus to produce landmark captions and VQA pairs (relative object position, color, robot orientation). The model is trained to caption and answer from the video up to the keyframe.

Flywheel loop: each round trains on half of the new error-correcting trajectories with their perception data, plus oracle trajectories equal to half that number for stability. The model is then re-evaluated on the train split for new errors. The loop is stopped when val performance drops (after 3 improving rounds). Cost is about 20 h per round on 8×A100, versus 80 h for fine-tuning.

setting.training_data: VLN-CE R2R+RxR train: >2.1M step-wise action samples (527K R2R, 1.58M RxR) with domain randomization; 30K trajectory→instruction samples (10K R2R, 20K RxR); 240K general video QA (ActivityNet-QA, NextQA from LLaVA-Video-178K). Then multi-round self-correction data auto-generated on the train split: planner-generated recovery trajectories plus Qwen-VL-Plus keyframe captions/VQA (about 3 flywheel rounds).
setting.observation: monocular RGB video (16 sampled frames) + instruction; no depth/panorama/odometry
setting.action_space: low-level discrete VLN-CE actions predicted as an action chunk of 4 actions (exact step sizes not stated); real robot calls quadruped motion API
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT reference paths on the train split are used only to build flywheel training data)

numbers_note: Per-iteration flywheel results (iterations 1-4, SR/NE on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen) are shown only in a line figure and are not included here. Table 2 gives exact numbers only for the 1st iteration. The paper does not report TL, nDTW on R2R-CE, or OSR on RxR-CE. Real-world SR is printed as fractions and converted to 0-100 here. The claimed '+8.2%/+16.4%' over StreamVLN are absolute SR points.
results: On VLN-CE val-unseen with monocular RGB only, CorrectNav reaches R2R-CE SR 65.1 / SPL 62.3 / NE 4.24 and RxR-CE SR 69.3 / SPL 63.3 / nDTW 75.2. This beats the strongest VLM-based baseline StreamVLN (56.9 / 52.9 SR) by 8.2 and 16.4 points, and the best waypoint-predictor method HNR (61.0 / 56.3 SR, which uses panoramic RGB-D + odometry). In real quadruped tests across office, home and campus, it reaches 0.75-0.95 SR versus 0.10-0.55 for NaVid and NaVILA, with the largest gains on complex instructions (e.g., Home complex 0.80 vs 0.15).
limitations: Monocular RGB gives imprecise body-to-surroundings geometry, so a quadruped's hind legs may scrape obstacles; robot body dimensions and state are not modeled.

The flywheel depends on simulator re-rollouts on the training split with GT reference paths and a trajectory planner. Each round costs about 20 h on 8×A100, and gains saturate/degrade after 3 rounds, with per-round numbers only in a figure.
Real-world evaluation is small (20 simple + 20 complex instructions per environment) and uses remote A100 inference. No test-server results are reported.
